correction:
The claim itself holds, but four supporting statements in the surveys are overstated or wrong and should not be carried into the plan:

1. "Static shards are 158x faster than pyarrow filtering" is measured against a strawman. That ratio uses the un-repartitioned single-row-group file. Against a correctly sorted+re-partitioned parquet, pyarrow is 2.8 ms vs the shard's 0.187 ms — about 15x, and both are far below any interactivity threshold. Static shards are the right choice for operational reasons (no server, no runtime, $0 hosting), NOT because parquet is too slow.

2. "Sort by gene_symbol and write row_group_size=8000" — the SORT is the load-bearing half and the surveys underplay it. Re-chunking the file as-is prunes nothing: gene_symbol is scattered within three region blocks, so all 112 row groups survive min/max pruning and 98.9% of the file is still read. Locality of a gene's rows (2.98 contiguous runs/gene) is not the same as statistics-prunability.

3. DuckDB-WASM / HTTP-range partial reads over the CURRENT files are a hard non-starter, and for a second reason the surveys never checked: neither large parquet has a page index (has_offset_index=False, has_column_index=False), so there is no sub-row-group page skipping to fall back on either. Also, duckdb is not merely "not installed" — it installs cleanly (1.5.5) and I measured it at 88.0 ms (original) / 11.7 ms (sorted), which makes it SLOWER than plain pyarrow on the sorted file (2.8 ms). DuckDB buys nothing here.

4. The in-memory server RAM figure of 782 MB is the DataFrame's deep memory, not the process footprint. Measured peak RSS for load+index was 1,667 MB. Any hosting-tier sizing must use ~1.7 GB, which excludes most 1 GB free tiers.

Two further caveats that change how the numbers should be read:
- All timings are warm-page-cache. This is conservative for shards (a cold 3 KB read is still one seek) and generous to the parquet paths (a cold 44 MB read is not free), so the shard advantage is a lower bound.
- Local read latency is not user-facing latency. Over HTTP a single round trip (~20-100 ms) dominates every difference between 0.187 ms, 2.8 ms and 11.7 ms. The real per-gene budget is one request for a ~3.3 KB gzipped shard, not the parse time.

One correction in the survey's favour: the scale survey's recommendation to avoid per-nucleotide DOM elements is stricter than the data requires. The worst case is 7,784 nodes and zero transcripts exceed 10,000, so per-residue rendering is viable — which preserves the option of per-nucleotide NTScore colouring on the 3'UTR track. Per-segment (max 379 nodes) remains the better default, and it is safe because overlapping motifs are provably absent (0 of 835,848 adjacent pairs), though 6.43% abut exactly and need a separator to avoid fusing into one false motif.
